issues.legal_issue: A municipality may retain property tax collected under an invalid assessment only to the extent that the tax has been assessed according to law.
material_facts: Property taxes were collected under assessments made using a valuation method that the Court had held invalid.
The governing amendment permitted reassessment under the amended rules and required previously collected amounts to be taken into account, with any excess refunded.
No assessment or reassessment in accordance with the amended provisions had been made when the appeals were heard.
issues.conclusion: The relevant provision did not authorize the municipality to retain amounts collected illegally before a lawful assessment or reassessment had been made.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 152A(1) and (2) of the Bombay Provincial Municipal Corporation Act, as amended, the municipality could reassess property tax under the amended provisions, take amounts already collected into account, and refund any excess. It could retain only tax assessed according to law; the section did not authorize retention of illegally collected amounts without such an assessment. The Court therefore found it unnecessary to examine the constitutional validity of section 152A itself.

rule.if: property_tax_refund_proceeding and tax_collected_under_invalid_assessment and not lawful_reassessment_completed

predicates.property_tax_refund_proceeding: A proceeding seeks the return of property tax collected by a municipality.
predicates.tax_collected_under_invalid_assessment: The municipality collected tax under an assessment made using a method that was held invalid.
predicates.lawful_reassessment_completed: The municipality completed an assessment or reassessment of the tax in accordance with the governing legal requirements.

issues.definition: When a property-tax refund proceeding concerns tax collected under an invalid assessment and no lawful reassessment has been completed, the municipality may not retain the unlawfully collected tax.

issues.legal_issue: A legislature cannot require a state instrumentality to disregard or disobey a court order, and cannot authorize retention of illegally collected tax as a forced loan.
material_facts: Court orders had required the return of property tax that had been illegally collected.
A later provision directed the municipality to withhold the refund despite those court orders until reassessment, while providing for interest on any amount ultimately found refundable.
The provision did not remove the basis of the court decisions and authorized the municipality to retain the collected amounts in the meantime.
issues.conclusion: The provision requiring the municipality to withhold refunds despite court orders was unconstitutional and was struck down.
issues.legal_principle: Legislatures may enact prospective or retrospective laws within constitutional limits and may remove the basis of a judicial decision, thereby making that decision ineffective in altered circumstances. They may not declare a court decision ineffective or require state instrumentalities to disregard it. The Court relied on Shri Prithvi Cotton Mills Ltd. v. Broach Borough Municipality, Mahal Chand Sethia v. State of West Bengal, Janpada Sabha, Chhindwara v. Central Provinces Syndicate Ltd., State of Madhya Pradesh v. Amalgamated Coal Fields Ltd., and State of Madhya Pradesh v. Ranojirao Shinde. It also held that authorizing the retention of illegally collected amounts as loans amounted to authorizing forced loans, which the Constitution does not permit.

predicates.constitutional_validity_challenge: A proceeding challenges the constitutional validity of a law.
predicates.law_compels_disregard_of_court_order: The law directs a state instrumentality to withhold a refund despite a court order requiring the refund, without removing the basis of that order.
predicates.law_authorizes_forced_loan: The law permits a state instrumentality to retain money illegally collected from a person and treat the retained amount as a loan.

issues.definition: A challenged law is unconstitutional when it requires a state instrumentality to disregard a court order or authorizes it to retain illegally collected money as a forced loan.
